tier_reason: The only numbers come from a competitor's vendor shootout (liquidaty/zsv app/benchmark/bench_quoting.sh), not a peer-reviewed paper or well-known independent suite, so B does not apply. Script, CPU (Apple M3 Pro) and xan version (0.54.1) are public, but the xan binary's compiler and flags are not stated, so it is not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: On zsv's darwin-arm64 shootout (Apple M3 Pro, xan 0.54.1, 500000x20 datasets, best-of-5), xan select takes 0.077s (unquoted) and 0.081s (sparse_quoted). Comparisons: xsv 0.189s/0.195s (~2.4x, derived from page data); single-threaded Polars 0.410s/0.408s; DuckDB default 0.110s/0.105s; single-threaded zsv fast 0.097s/0.105s. That makes xan the fastest single-threaded tool there, not the fastest overall: zsv fast --parallel (0.036s/0.035s), zsv compat --parallel (0.044s/0.047s) and, on sparse_quoted, DuckDB QUOTE='' (0.066s) are faster. xan count on unquoted: 0.023s, tied with zsv fast, vs xsv 0.087s. xan is N/A (incorrect output) on nonstandard_quoted data. On the Linux Xeon Platinum 8488C page (xan 0.56.0), xan select on unquoted takes 0.082s vs xsv 0.600s.
corrections.hardware: Apple M3 Pro (darwin-arm64 results page); a separate linux-x86_64 page uses Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C (zsv/xsv/xan/qsv only, no DuckDB/Polars)
corrections.caveats: Evidence comes from a competitor's (liquidaty/zsv) own shootout, not an independent well-known suite; the xan binary's build/compiler flags are not stated. Per its README, xan is originally a fork of BurntSushi/xsv, nearly entirely rewritten and not marked as a GitHub fork, so the xsv baseline is its own ancestor. The DuckDB version used is old (v0.10.2) and Polars was run single-threaded. xan produces incorrect output on nonstandard-quoted data. xan's parser is medialab/simd-csv (a separate record).

notes: The claim that xan is 'the fastest tool for select' was overstated: it is fastest only among single-threaded tools, and zsv --parallel variants beat it. Tier B->C because a competitor's vendor benchmark is not a well-known independent suite. Metadata checked: Unlicense (OSI-approved; no patent grant), 4527 stars, last commit 2026-09-23.

tier_reason: First-party results page generated by the public app/benchmark/bench_quoting.sh, with CPU (Apple M3 Pro) and tool versions stated. The script takes a prebuilt zsv binary and no compiler or flags are stated, so it is not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: On the darwin-arm64 page (Apple M3 Pro, best-of-5), count on unquoted data: zsv fast --parallel 0.008s (14.29 GB/s) vs DuckDB default 0.085s, DuckDB QUOTE='' (no quote recognition) 0.049s, and single-threaded Polars 0.092s (~10.6x vs DuckDB default, ~11.5x vs Polars, derived from page data); single-threaded zsv fast 0.023s vs DuckDB 1-thread QUOTE='' 0.112s. select on unquoted: zsv fast --parallel 0.036s vs DuckDB 0.110s and Polars 0.410s; single-threaded zsv fast (0.097s) is slower than xan (0.077s). The memory claim (1.5MB footprint, 52x smaller than DuckDB, 324x smaller than Polars, single-threaded) is on app/benchmark/README.md, not on the results page.
corrections.workload: count (row counting) and select (full parse + CSV re-output) on four synthetic 500000-row x 20-col datasets (~118-127MB: unquoted, ~2% sparse-quoted, ~20% RFC-4180 quoted, ~27% nonstandard mid-cell quotes), best-of-5, single- and multi-threaded, via app/benchmark/bench_quoting.sh; the 433MB worldcitiespop setup is described separately in app/benchmark/README.md
corrections.hardware: Apple M3 Pro (darwin-arm64 results page); a separate linux-x86_64 page uses Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C but excludes DuckDB and Polars
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark (liquidaty/zsv); the zsv binary's compiler and flags are not stated. The DuckDB version used is old (v0.10.2), and zsv's README reports ~100x DuckDB run-to-run variance with only minimum times used. Polars was run single-threaded via Python. The fastest SIMD 'zsv fast' parser gives incorrect output on nonstandard-quoted data (the compat parser is correct but slower). xan beats single-threaded zsv on select for unquoted and sparse data.
